reading.ours: two units of arithmetic per iteration
reading.floor: one unit of arithmetic per iteration
reading.caveat: NOT A PRICE — an instrument check, and it is printed first because nothing below it means anything until it passes. The true ratio is a little UNDER 2: both sides pay the driving loop once, so the exact expectation is (2u + L) / (u + L) with L the loop and u one unit, which at sixteen dependent steps per unit puts it around 1.9. A reading below 1.5 means this process could not resolve a deliberate doubling, and the runner voids the report rather than printing prices under it.

reading.ours: one unit of arithmetic per iteration
reading.floor: the same body again, over its own copy of the same state
reading.caveat: NOT A PRICE — the noise floor. The two sides are identical code over identical, separately-allocated state, so the true ratio is 1.00 exactly and every departure from it printed here was produced by this machine at this moment. The rule that follows is the one the whole table is read under: NO RATIO CLOSER TO 1.00 THAN THIS GAP IS A READING. It also bounds the per-row noise figure, which is the same idea measured again inside every pair — each pair times its floor twice, once before our side and once after, and prints how far the two disagreed.

reading.ours: slot.cache[column] — per-slot state read off the identity you already hold
reading.floor: REJECTED: stateBySlot.get(slot) — a WeakMap keyed by the identity
reading.caveat: WHAT THE REJECTED DESIGN WOULD HAVE BOUGHT, first, because it is the reason somebody proposed it: a WeakMap keyed by the identity keeps the state with WHOEVER MADE IT. Drop the map and the entire cache goes without touching a single slot; two consumers can never land on the same storage; and an entry vanishes on its own once nothing else holds the slot, so a churning population leaves nothing behind. A cell on the carrier has none of that — it outlives the consumer that wrote it, two consumers naming one column overwrite each other, and only `forget` or the slot's own death removes it. This row prices the ONE property the carrier has, addressing, and nothing else; the lifetime question is not a ratio and is not settled here. WHERE THE TWO ARE NOT EQUAL. (1) Ours is the shipped `cache` cell — a field load, an undefined check and an element load — which is the MORE expensive of the engine's two per-carrier shapes: a declared field such as `slot.linkCount` is one load and no check, so the engine's own per-carrier reads are cheaper than what is priced here as ours. Pushes the ratio up, against us. (2) Both sides walk the same slot array with the same mask, so an identical array load sits in the numerator and the denominator, and adding the same constant to both pulls a ratio below 1 toward 1 — it understates the gap. (3) Every cell is filled and every key hits, so neither side takes a miss branch. (4) The WeakMap holds 8192 live entries. Our cost does not move with population size and a hash table's does, so this ratio is not a constant: a smaller population flatters the floor, a larger one flatters us. (5) THIS IS NOT THE FASTEST SIDE MAP THERE IS — a non-weak `Map` keyed by the slot skips the weak-reference bookkeeping, and it is priced separately below precisely so this row cannot be accused of having picked the floor that loses.

reading.ours: slot.cache[column] — per-slot state read off the identity you already hold
reading.floor: REJECTED: stateBySlot.get(slot) — a plain Map keyed by the identity
reading.caveat: THE CONTROL ON THE ROW ABOVE, and the reason it exists is that nobody would ship this one. A non-weak `Map` keyed by the slot retains every identity it has ever been shown for the life of the process, which is the leak the WeakMap exists to prevent — so what this design would have bought is nothing a person wants, and it is here as an instrument rather than as a candidate. What it IS, is the fastest object-keyed side map V8 offers. So: the distance between this ratio and the WeakMap ratio is what WEAKNESS costs, and this ratio alone is what side-map ADDRESSING costs with the lifetime question set aside entirely. If our side does not beat this floor, the addressing argument has not been made and the WeakMap row was measuring the weak references rather than the design. Every inequality listed on the row above applies here unchanged except its last point: the identical array load in both bodies, the undefined check charged only to us, the all-hit population, and the fact that our cost is flat in the population size while a hash table's is not.

reading.ours: slot.cache[column] — per-slot state read off the identity you already hold
reading.floor: REJECTED: stateByKey.get(row.id) — a Map keyed by the primary key
reading.caveat: WHAT THE REJECTED DESIGN WOULD HAVE BOUGHT: the state is reachable WITHOUT holding the identity. A key out of a URL, a server payload or a dispatched action reaches it directly, nothing has to have resolved a slot first, and the state survives the slot entirely — which is exactly what you want for something keyed by an id that has not arrived yet. The cell cannot do any of that, and this row is the price of the convenience rather than a verdict on it. WHERE THE TWO ARE NOT EQUAL. Both sides do one array load and then one field load — `slot.cache` against `row.id` — and diverge only after it, which is what makes this the clean statement of the identity principle. Against us: our undefined check, again charged to nobody else. In the floor's favour, and this is the big one: V8 memoises a string's hash in the string header on first use, and these are the SAME string objects on every pass of every sample, so the floor never once pays to hash a fresh key — which is precisely what a real application does when the key came out of a JSON parse or a template literal. Direction: understates the gap, and by more than any other item in this file. Read this row beside `find.vs-map-get`: that one prices resolving a key to an identity ONCE, this one prices the alternative to having done so, per read, for ever.

THE CHEAPEST ROW IN THIS FILE TO WRITE HONESTLY, because both sides are classes this package already ships and neither had to be reconstructed from a comment. Note what that makes it: the WeakMap side is NOT a rejected design at all — both are exported and documented, and the choice between them is a consumer's. What was rejected is only the claim that they cost the same. WHAT THE WEAK ONE BUYS is written on its own class and is real: the cache belongs to whoever made it and dies with them, two consumers can never collide, and entries vanish as the population churns — where a cell outlives its writer and two consumers naming one column overwrite each other. WHERE THE TWO ARE NOT EQUAL. Each side is one method call on a receiver of exactly one class, from its own call site, so both are monomorphic — which is also what a consumer holding one of the two gets, so this is not an artificial advantage for either. The call overhead is on both sides and pulls the ratio toward 1, understating whatever gap exists. Ours additionally loads `this.column` and takes the undefined check on `slot.cache`; the floor loads `this.byRow`. Every slot is populated in both, so no miss branch runs on either side. Population-size direction as elsewhere: our cost is flat in it, a WeakMap's is not. AND THE FIGURE THIS REPLACES: two source files, the package README, `llms.txt` and two docs pages all state 3.677 ns against 8.887 on a 0.117 ns floor. Nothing here subtracts a floor from either side — the two absolute nanosecond figures the report prints are what the process measured, and the ratio is theirs.

reading.ours: fill four populations of ONE collection class — 8192 upserts
reading.floor: REJECTED: fill four populations of FOUR empty subclasses — 8192 upserts
reading.caveat: WHAT THE REJECTED DESIGN WOULD HAVE BOUGHT: `groupBy`, `groupByEach`, `groupByCompositeKey` and `all` as METHODS. Discoverable by typing a dot on the population, typed to it without a generic argument, and with no free function for a caller to find and import. That is the DX the four free functions gave up, and it is not a small thing to give up. Note that the free-function decision ALSO rests on a bundling argument — a class body cannot be partially tree-shaken, so a method that constructs its strategies inline pins them into every consumer — which this row does not measure and which does not depend on what it reports. THE GEOMETRY IS HELD STILL, and that is what makes this pair different from the experiment behind the +76% nobody can find. Both sides run FOUR populations of 2048 rows: same total rows, same total writes, same number of populations, same key selector object, same database options, same loop. One population of N against four of N/4 would have been a different experiment, whose split moves the number on its own — so the split is on both sides and cancels, and what is left between them is how many hidden classes the engine sees. The subclasses are EMPTY because the claim says the price is the shape and not the methods; bodies would measure the bodies too. THIS DOES NOT REPRODUCE THE ORIGINAL EXPERIMENT and cannot: nothing records what it did. `website/docs/performance/index.md` already carries the verdict that +76% is unsupported and that the +14% offered to correct it is too. This row replaces both rather than adjudicating between them. THIS PAIR DECLARES `isolate`, AND IT IS THE REASON THAT CAPABILITY EXISTS. Both sides call the SAME compiled `OIMCollection` methods, whose inline caches belong to their call sites and not to the receiver. Measured the ordinary way — both sides built and timed in one process — those caches would have seen all five maps by the time our side ran, the base class and the four subclasses, and our side would be measured through caches the rejected design spoiled. That does not merely bias the number, it makes it UNREADABLE: a ratio at 1.00 would be equally consistent with "the shape costs nothing" and with "the other arm spoiled the caches ours ran through". So each side is probed and timed in a process that has never constructed the other, five processes in all, and `build` is told which side is wanted — declining to TIME the other design is not enough, because merely FILLING its populations teaches V8 its shape. What remains charged honestly is the timed body's own call site: ours dispatches to one map there and the floor to four, which is exactly what a consumer of four subclasses would have had. The residual cost is that `noise` now includes process-to-process variation, which is the honest thing for it to include here. Each side gets its OWN database, so no flush ever walks the other side's frame, and each pass ends with exactly one flush per 8192 rows. Both sides abandon their four populations between passes and the collection runs outside the clock.
